mstts:express-as.prosody: Imagine stepping into a world where the wisdom of plants and the wonders of science come together—inviting us to see the earth with fresh eyes. As we explore Braiding Sweetgrass: Indigenous Wisdom, Scientific Knowledge, and the Teachings of Plants, Robin Wall Kimmerer gently guides us to a place where gratitude, reciprocity, and deep respect for all living things truly matter. Throughout her story, Kimmerer weaves together her experiences as both a botanist and a member of the Citizen Potawatomi Nation. She shows us how sweetgrass—a plant held sacred by many—becomes more than just a symbol. It’s a living reminder of how different strands of wisdom can come together, each one making the whole a bit stronger. As we walk alongside her through forests and fields, we begin to see the natural world as a generous teacher. Plants quietly share lessons about resilience, generosity, and how deeply connected we all are. This journey asks us to pay attention—to the turning seasons, to the voices of elders, and to the stories written in the land itself. We’re invited to listen, to learn, and to honor the gifts the earth offers each of us. In this space, braiding sweetgrass is more than just a task—it’s a gesture of hope, of healing, and of finding our place in the web of life. So, together, let’s open our hearts and curiosity as we discover how science and indigenous wisdom can come together, teaching us how to live in harmony with the earth and one another.

Chapter 1: Learning to See the World as a Gift
Have you ever noticed how some mornings just feel different? The air’s a little crisper, and it almost seems like the world is quietly offering you something—like a gentle invitation you can feel but can’t quite explain. Maybe it’s just the dew shining on the grass, or the peaceful hush among the trees.
For a lot of us, the day kicks off in a rush—alarms blaring, a pile of tasks waiting, and that familiar weight of everything we need to get done. But if you’ve ever grown up with stories that connect people to the land, or even just spent a little time really paying attention to the world outside, mornings can start with something else: gratitude.
Now, I don’t mean the kind of gratitude that feels forced or like some daily obligation. I’m talking about a real, simple thankfulness—just for being here, for the sunlight streaming in, for another chance to see what the day brings.
Picture a family where a child learns to greet each morning, not by checking off a list, but with a quiet acknowledgment: hey, the world itself is a gift. And this isn’t just a lesson for kids—it’s a way of seeing that sticks with you as you grow. When you look at the world as a gift, suddenly every plant, every animal, even every rainstorm feels like something to cherish, not just use up.
The truth is, most of us, especially if we live in busy cities, don’t really notice this. It’s easy to see the world as just stuff—resources to own, things to consume. But in some traditions, the land isn’t just ground beneath our feet. It’s alive. We’re part of its family, not separate from it. And that subtle shift changes everything. Instead of asking, “What can I take?” you start to wonder, “What can I give in return?”
This way of thinking isn’t just about being polite to nature—it’s about recognizing a relationship. In some homes, for instance, the very first strawberries of the season aren’t eaten right away. They’re offered back to the earth, as a small thank you. It’s this gentle reminder that nothing is truly ours—everything is shared.
There’s a story I love about a young person, eager to pick wild berries, who’s stopped by an elder. The elder doesn’t scold, but quietly asks if the berries have been greeted, if thanks have been given. It’s not about following rules—it’s about showing respect. Those berries, after all, aren’t just food. They’re relatives. Teachers. Gifts.
Over time, this way of seeing the world starts to shape how people act. Gratitude becomes more than just a feeling—it becomes a habit. It influences every choice, big or small. When you see the world as a gift, wasting things just feels wrong. Taking care comes naturally, and the land stops being just a backdrop—it becomes a living presence in your life.
And here’s the beautiful part: this perspective isn’t tied to any one culture or place. Anyone—you, me, anyone—can learn to see the world this way. It starts with the smallest acts: maybe pausing before you pick a flower, taking a second to notice how the wind moves through the leaves, or just saying a quiet thank you before a meal.
These tiny moments? They add up. Over time, they weave a whole new kind of relationship with the world around you. And that, I think, is a gift in itself.

Let’s wander together into Chapter Two: Plants as Teachers and Relatives.
Picture yourself walking through a forest—not as just another passerby, but truly among family. The trees? They’re not just silent observers or background scenery. They’re elders, each one filled with stories and wisdom, waiting to share—if only we know how to listen.
For some folks, seeing the world this way comes naturally. For others, it’s a gentle shift in perspective—one that grows with time and a little bit of practice.
In certain communities, kids learn early on that plants aren’t just things. They’re living beings, each with their own intelligence, their own way of moving through the world. Imagine a child watching a maple tree. She notices how it waits for that perfect moment to send out its leaves, or how it quietly shares its sugar with everyone. These aren’t just interesting facts—they become lessons in patience, generosity, and timing.
There’s this memory of students, hands deep in the soil, planting seeds together. Some of them want results, fast. But the garden? It teaches at its own pace. Seeds need time, warmth, and care—no shortcuts. Soon, the students start noticing those tiny changes: a sprout breaking through, roots stretching for water. Slowly, the garden transforms into a classroom, and the plants become the quietest, but wisest, of teachers.
Picture a family out in the springtime, gathering wild leeks. They pick just what they need, leaving plenty behind. The youngest asks, “Why not take more?” An older relative smiles, explaining the leeks aren’t just food—they’re neighbors. If you take too many, the patch won’t come back. The lesson is simple: take only what you can give back.
This kind of learning? It’s not about memorizing lists or facts. It’s all about building relationships. Plants teach simply by being themselves: a sunflower turning toward the sun, moss holding onto water, beans climbing and supporting each other. Each one quietly shares lessons in adaptation, teamwork, and resilience.
Most people have no idea how much plants are aware. Scientists have watched beans in the lab, seeing how they reach out, searching for something to climb. Put a pole nearby? The bean finds it. If there’s nothing, it just keeps searching. That persistence is a gentle reminder—life keeps adapting, always finding connection.
In many cultures, plants are called “the oldest teachers.” They’ve been around far longer than we have, and their wisdom is woven into the landscape itself. Learning from them isn’t about copying exactly what they do—it’s about listening. Really tuning in to the rhythms of growth, the cycles of giving and receiving.
And this way of learning truly changes everything. Instead of seeing plants as just resources, we begin to see them as mentors, guides. Their lessons aren’t flashy, but they last. They show us patience, generosity, and why community matters. They remind us that we’re all part of a greater web, where every action ripples out and matters.
Over time, these lessons shape how we live. They call us to be humble, curious, and respectful. They invite us to slow down, to notice, and to care more deeply. In a world that often pushes for speed and control, the teachings of plants offer us a different path—a path rooted in relationship, reciprocity, and a true sense of belonging.

Let’s dive into Chapter 3: Blending Indigenous Knowledge and Science.
Have you ever felt like you’re living in two very different worlds at once? Maybe in school, you’re surrounded by the language of science—data, experiments, and measurements. But at home, the stories you hear are rich with tradition, music, and ceremony. For people who walk between these two worlds, something truly special can happen.
Picture this: A student sits through a botany lecture, hearing all about photosynthesis. The professor’s explanation is crystal clear—full of chemical equations and big words. It’s impressive, sure, but somehow, it feels a little... incomplete. Later that day, the same student listens to an elder at home, who describes how plants make food from sunlight, water, and air. But this time, it’s not just about the science. It’s about the miracle of life itself. Less about hard facts, more about wonder.
At first, these two ways of understanding the world might seem like they just don’t mix. Science is all about objectivity and proof. Indigenous knowledge is rooted in relationships and meaning. But here’s what’s fascinating—over time, you start to realize that both perspectives have something truly valuable to offer.
Imagine a research lab where scientists are studying sweetgrass. They’re busy measuring soil, sunlight, and water to find patterns. Meanwhile, out in the field, traditional harvesters are carefully gathering sweetgrass, paying close attention to how the plant responds. They’ve noticed something: if sweetgrass is harvested with care, it actually thrives. If it’s left alone or overharvested, it fades away. The scientists’ data ends up confirming what the harvesters already knew—sweetgrass needs to be used, not ignored.
That’s pretty powerful, isn’t it? It shows us that science and traditional knowledge aren’t rivals. They’re partners, each seeing the world through a different lens. Science helps explain how things work. Traditional knowledge shows us why they matter.
There’s a great story about a group of students—some trained in science, others in traditional ways—who come together to restore a wetland. At first, it’s tough. The scientists want to measure everything. The traditionalists want to just listen to the land. But as they work together, something changes. The scientists start slowing down, picking up on subtle signs of a healthy ecosystem. The traditionalists learn how data can help track changes over time. In the end, their restoration plan honors both ways of knowing.
Blending these different forms of knowledge isn’t always easy. It asks us to be humble, patient, and open to truly listening. It means letting go of the idea that one way is better than the other. Instead, it’s about finding common ground, and realizing that both science and traditional knowledge are driven by the same things—curiosity and care.
And here’s the real takeaway: When we blend these approaches, we get new insights. We see just how complex the world really is, and that no single way of knowing is ever quite enough. This kind of learning inspires collaboration, creativity, and respect. It’s a reminder that learning isn’t just about gathering facts—it’s about building real relationships. With each other, and with the land itself.

Chapter 4: Reciprocity and Responsibility in Everyday Life
There’s a quiet kind of joy that comes from giving back—a feeling of balance, like you’re really part of something bigger than yourself.
For a lot of folks, reciprocity is just a word—maybe something you remember from a class or overheard in conversation.
But for people who live close to the land, reciprocity is so much more—it's a way of being.
Picture this: in one home, giving thanks isn’t just a routine or some mindless tradition. Before every meal, someone pauses—not because they have to, but because they truly appreciate what’s on their plate.
Those vegetables? They’re not just calories to be counted. They’re gifts from the garden—made possible by sunlight, rain, and a whole lot of care.
Eating becomes a little ceremony; a moment to connect, and to remember that nothing is ever just “given.”
There’s another memory I want to share—a group of friends gathering wild rice from a quiet lake.
It’s slow work, and it takes patience. But that’s the point. Everyone only takes what they need, making sure there’s plenty left for others—whether that’s people or animals.
They laugh and swap stories while they work. And at the end of the day, they return some of the rice to the water—a simple gesture, but one filled with gratitude and respect.
This kind of living isn’t about strict rules or duties. It’s about recognizing that we’re all part of a web—a big, beautiful network of relationships.
Whenever we take, we give. Whenever we receive, we express thanks.
Of course, keeping that balance isn’t always easy—especially in a world that often pushes us to gather and store more, instead of sharing.
In some communities, there’s a guiding idea called the “Honorable Harvest.”
The rules? They’re simple: take only what you need, use everything you take, share with others, and always give thanks.
These aren’t written down—they’re passed from one generation to the next, shaping how people hunt, fish, gather, and grow with respect.
I think about a young person learning to fish for the first time—so excited by the catch. But then, an older relative gently reminds them: thank the fish, use every part, and share the meal.
It’s not about feeling guilty. It’s about feeling grateful—understanding that the fish is a gift, and that gifts come with responsibility.
Over time, living this way really changes how you see things.
The land stops being something to conquer or control. It starts to feel like a partner, a relative—your source of life.
Suddenly, you start noticing all the little ways you can give back—planting a tree, picking up trash from a stream, sharing your harvest with neighbors.
These acts might seem tiny, but they add up. They help build a culture of care.
Most people don’t realize just how much these small gestures matter.
When gratitude and reciprocity become part of your daily life, they shape your community. They create a sense of belonging—a feeling that everyone has something important to offer.
And maybe, most importantly, they remind us that the world isn’t just a place to live. It’s a home to care for.

Chapter 5: Healing Through Restoration and Stewardship
Let's talk about something deeper than just repairing what's broken. Restoration goes beyond fixing things—it's really about mending relationships. Not just with the land, but with each other, and even with those parts of ourselves we've set aside or forgotten.
Now, stewardship—what does that word even mean to most people? Sometimes, it can feel distant or maybe like it's only for experts and activists. But if you've grown up close to the land, you know stewardship is a daily act. It's woven from love, responsibility, and the simple routines of caring for what surrounds us.
Picture this: a small community, neighbors rolling up their sleeves to restore a neglected pond. The water’s cloudy, weeds everywhere, and hardly any fish left. At first, it feels like an impossible job. But little by little, as they clear debris, plant native flowers, and make space for wildlife, the pond slowly starts to heal. And here's the beautiful part—so do the people working beside it.
Or think about a family returning to an old homestead. The fields are tangled with weeds, and the soil feels worn out. But they start simple—maybe just planting a garden, tending the old trees, listening to the rhythm of the earth. Over time, the land wakes up. Birds come back. Wildflowers color the fields. And the family? They discover a sense of belonging that’s way deeper than just owning property.
Restoration isn’t only about bringing the land back to life. It’s also about restoring our connections—with our ancestors, with those who’ll come after us, and with all the living beings who share this world. In some cultures, people are taught to think seven generations ahead—to imagine how today’s choices will ripple out for those not even born yet. That long view? It makes you slow down, care more, choose patience.
In classrooms, students are learning about ecological restoration. Sure, they study the science—but they also hear the stories. Maybe they visit a prairie, see how fire, grazing, and time work together to shape the land. They meet elders who remember when the prairie was bursting with life, and who share memories of abundance. That’s when the students realize: restoration isn’t just technical. It’s cultural, emotional, and even spiritual.
Most of us don’t realize just how much healing is possible. Even the smallest acts—planting a single tree, cleaning up a stream, tending a patch of garden—can spark change. These aren’t just ways to fix problems. They’re ways to create hope. They remind us that everyone has a part to play, and that healing can happen, even when things feel lost.
Over time, stewardship becomes more than a habit—it becomes a way of seeing the world. You stop thinking of yourself as an owner, and start to feel like a caretaker. It asks for humility, patience, and a willingness to really listen. And most of all, it reminds us that the land isn’t just a resource. It’s a relative—worthy of respect, attention, and care.

Chapter 6: The Language of Plants and the Power of Story
There’s a quiet kind of magic in the way stories move through our lives. Have you ever noticed how they get passed along—sometimes whispered, sometimes sung, always connecting one person to another? For a lot of people, language is just a way to get a point across. But if you really listen, you’ll find it’s so much more—it’s a bridge to the living world around us.
The words we choose shape the way we see everything. They determine what we notice, what we value. In some families, you’ll find children growing up hearing the names of plants spoken with care. Each name is like a small gift—a piece of history, a relationship, even a promise tucked inside every syllable.
Picture a grandmother kneeling in her garden, teaching her grandchild the names of the plants growing all around them. She doesn’t just point and label; she tells stories. She talks about how milkweed feeds the monarch butterflies, how beans climb with hope, how sweetgrass braids itself into the earth. The child listens, repeating the names, feeling the weight and wonder of each one. Suddenly, you realize—language isn’t just about describing things. It’s a way of honoring, remembering, belonging.
Here’s something people often miss: when a language disappears, we lose so much more than just words. The names of plants, the stories about their gifts, the songs that call them back in spring—these are threads in a living tapestry. When those threads break, a way of seeing the world—of knowing what’s possible—fades with them.
Imagine a classroom where a teacher invites students to learn the names of local plants, not just in English, but in the language of the land’s first people. At first, the new words feel strange on their tongues. But gradually, those sounds become familiar, like old friends. The students start to realize that some names actually describe what a plant does, how it feels, or the way it dances in the wind. Suddenly, language becomes a kind of map, guiding them toward deeper understanding.
There’s a story about a young person who, after years away, returns home and tries to remember the plant names they once knew. At first, the words come slowly. But with each name, a memory returns—a taste, a smell, a feeling of home. It’s clear that learning the language of plants isn’t just about memorizing vocabulary. It’s about building relationships. It’s about coming home—to yourself, and to the land itself.
Over time, the power of story and language weaves us back into the world. It reminds us we’re not alone—that every plant, every animal, every stone has a story to share, if only we’ll listen. Language challenges us to pay attention, to learn, and to pass along what we know. In this way, it becomes a true gift—a way of keeping the world alive, one story, one name at a time.

Chapter 7: Ceremony, Gratitude, and the Practice of Belonging.
There are those moments in life that really call for ceremony. I’m not talking about big, formal events, but the quieter rituals that mark our days—the way we notice the seasons changing, the times we gather with friends, or even just the simple act of giving thanks.
For a lot of us, ceremony might seem like something reserved for rare occasions. But if you live close to the land, you know it’s part of everyday life, woven into the smallest moments.
Picture this: a family stands at the edge of a lake, baskets in hand, ready to collect wild rice. But before they start, they pause. Someone sings a song. Someone else sprinkles tobacco on the water—a gesture of gratitude for the rice, the water, the sun overhead.
It’s such a simple ceremony, but it transforms everything. Suddenly, harvesting rice isn’t just a chore—it becomes a way of belonging. It’s a way of saying, “We’re here, and we’re thankful.”
Most people don’t realize just how much ceremony shapes the way we see the world. It’s not about following rules, or ticking boxes—it’s about paying attention. It’s about being present.
Ceremony invites us to slow down, to really notice what’s around us—to remember that we’re part of something much bigger.
Let me share another story. Imagine a group of friends gathering for a meal. Before anyone picks up a fork, they take just a moment to thank the plants and animals that made the meal possible. The words are plain, but the feeling? It’s real. And you know what? The food tastes different—richer, somehow more alive.
That’s when you realize gratitude isn’t just something you feel—it’s something you do. The more you practice it, the deeper it goes.
There’s also the memory of a child learning to plant corn. The planting isn’t rushed—it’s done with songs and prayers, with real care for the seeds and the earth. The child might not grasp every word, but still senses the meaning—in the rhythm, in the gentle touch, in the attention to every detail.
What that child learns over time is that ceremony isn’t about getting everything perfect. It’s about intention. It’s a way of showing respect, of leaving room for a little wonder.
In all its forms, ceremony becomes a way of belonging. It reminds us that we’re not separate from the world—we’re part of its ongoing story. It nudges us to give thanks, to care, to remember where we are and who we’re with.
In a world that often moves too fast and sometimes feels disconnected, ceremony gives us a way back—to gratitude, to relationship, to a sense of home.

Chapter 8: The Honorable Harvest—Living with Limits
You know, there’s a kind of wisdom that comes from living close to the edge, where resources aren’t endless and every choice really counts. Most of us think of limits as something that holds us back—something to push past or conquer. But if you listen to people who’ve learned from the land, you’ll find that limits aren’t barriers at all. They’re guides, quietly pointing us in the right direction.
Picture this: a group of people heads into the forest, baskets in hand, ready to gather mushrooms. There’s a real buzz in the air—everyone’s hoping to find that perfect patch. But before anyone starts, an elder steps forward and gently reminds them of something called the Honorable Harvest. The rules are simple: only take what you need, never pick the first one you see, always leave some behind for others, and don’t forget to give thanks. These aren’t just empty words—they completely change the way people move through the world.
It’s surprisingly easy to take too much, isn’t it? We forget that this world is shared, not just with other people, but with all living things. The Honorable Harvest isn’t about going without or feeling deprived. It’s about finding balance—a way of living that recognizes everyone’s needs, human and more-than-human alike.
Let me tell you another story. Imagine a family fishing on a river that’s fed them for generations. One year, the fish just aren’t as plentiful, and it’d be so tempting to take a little extra, just in case. But the family remembers old stories—stories about lean years and why it’s so important to leave enough for the future. So, they only take what they need, and because of that, the river keeps on giving.
Or think of a child out picking berries for the first time. The child’s eager to fill their basket to the brim, but an older relative gently shows them something different: how to leave a few berries for the birds, some for the bears, and even some for the plants themselves. The lesson isn’t about scarcity—it’s about generosity. Living with limits, it turns out, isn’t a burden at all. It’s a gift. It means there’s always enough to go around.
Over time, the Honorable Harvest becomes more than just a set of rules—it’s a way of life. It shapes every choice we make, whether big or small. It invites us to ask, “What’s enough?”—and then to really listen for the answer. It reminds us that true abundance isn’t about having more, but about sharing well.
When we live with limits, we find a path to freedom, to joy, and to belonging. And maybe, just maybe, that’s the greatest gift of all.

Chapter 9: Sweetgrass—A Story of Resilience and Renewal.
Sweetgrass isn’t just a plant. It’s a story, a teacher, and a symbol of incredible resilience. For so many people, sweetgrass weaves its way into daily life—the scent drifting through the air, the braids serving as gentle reminders of home and connection.
But here’s something easy to forget: sweetgrass is also delicate. It’s threatened by overharvesting, by shrinking habitats, and sometimes, just by being forgotten.
Imagine a group of people coming together, determined to restore a patch of sweetgrass that’s almost vanished. The work is slow—pulling out stubborn weeds, gently planting new shoots, taking care of the soil. At first, it feels overwhelming, maybe even impossible. But as the seasons pass, something amazing happens. The sweetgrass returns, its green blades shimmering in the sunlight.
There’s a special moment when the people gather for the first harvest. Hands move in rhythm, braiding the sweetgrass, hearts filled with hope for what’s growing back.
Most of us don’t realize just how much care it takes to bring something back to life. Restoration isn’t only about putting new plants in the ground—it’s about building a relationship. Sweetgrass flourishes when it’s gathered with respect, when people use it thoughtfully and honor its presence. But when it’s neglected, or taken without care, it fades away.
There’s this wonderful story of a child learning to braid sweetgrass for the very first time. The strands keep slipping through their fingers, and weaving the pattern feels tricky. An elder steps in, showing them how to be patient, how to really listen to the plant, how to let the gentle rhythm lead their hands. Slowly, the braid takes shape—strong, beautiful, and full of meaning.
That’s when it becomes clear: resilience isn’t about never breaking. It’s about learning to weave together what’s left, finding strength in what remains.
Over time, sweetgrass turns into a powerful symbol of renewal. It reminds everyone that healing truly is possible—that even things lost to us can return, if we care for them with patience and love. Sweetgrass gently encourages us to keep trying, to keep tending, and to hold on to hope.
In the end, sweetgrass teaches us that resilience is more than a personal trait—it’s a collective practice. It’s about coming together, weaving new possibilities from old threads, and finding beauty in what we’re able to restore, together.

Chapter 10: Weaving Together—Science, Story, and the Work of Hope.
There’s a moment when everything just... comes together. Science, story, tradition, hope—all these threads that once felt separate suddenly begin to weave into something new. Have you ever noticed how divided the world can feel? Like there are different camps, each with their own way of knowing, their own way of living?
But if you’ve learned to braid, to weave, or even just to listen—really listen—a whole new pattern starts to reveal itself.
Picture this: a group of students out on a restoration project. They’re measuring soil and water, collecting scientific data. But that’s not all—they’re also gathering stories from elders, listening to the songs carried by the land. At first, it’s a little awkward. The pieces don’t quite fit. But as time goes on, a rhythm develops. The students start to trust one another, to value each unique perspective. They begin to see the world not as a patchwork of separate pieces, but as a living, breathing braid.
Most people don’t realize just how much strength comes from weaving together different ways of knowing. Science gives us tools, methods, explanations—sure. But story? Story brings meaning, connection, and purpose. When you put them together, you get something stronger, more resilient, and honestly, more true than either could be on their own.
There’s a memory that stands out: a community gathering to celebrate the restoration of a wetland. Scientists are there sharing data, elders telling stories, children splashing in the water. The celebration isn’t only about what’s been accomplished—it’s about what becomes possible when people work together. And suddenly, you realize that hope isn't just a feeling. It’s a practice. It’s about showing up, caring, and believing in the future—even when it’s uncertain.
Over time, this weaving of science and story becomes more than a project—it becomes a way of life. It shapes how we see ourselves: not as outsiders looking in, but as part of the world’s ongoing creation. It encourages us to keep learning, to keep listening, to keep braiding new possibilities together.
So, the work of hope? It’s not a solo act. It’s a shared journey—one that’s never truly finished, but always, always beginning.

As we wrap up our journey through Braiding Sweetgrass, I hope you’re noticing the world with fresh eyes. The heart of these stories isn’t just about plants or science or tradition—it’s about building relationships. It’s all about learning to see life as a gift, tuning in to what the land is quietly teaching us, and finding where you truly belong in this beautiful web we all share. So, what really matters here? Gratitude—it’s something you can practice every day, deepening your connection to the world around you. Remember, plants and land aren’t just resources; they’re relatives and teachers, worthy of our respect. When you blend science with Indigenous wisdom, you get a much richer, more caring way of understanding. Ceremony and story help us remember our place, and what we owe to each other. And living with limits—being mindful about what you take and what you give back—makes sure there’s enough for everyone, now and for the future. To bring this all together, just know that every small act of care truly counts. You don’t have to be an expert or stand on a stage to make a difference. Start simple: notice the gifts that surround you, offer thanks to the land, and share what you can. Listen to the stories that others carry, and share your own. Get curious—learn the names of the plants and animals that share your home. Try practicing the Honorable Harvest: take only what you need, and always give something back. The world is out there, waiting for your attention, your care, and your hope. Real healing—for the land and for ourselves—happens when we choose to live in relationship, with humility, patience, and love. The braid isn’t ever finished. Every day, you have a chance to add a new strand—to help weave a future where people and the earth can thrive together. So let your actions, no matter how small, become part of that ongoing story.
